claims.nodeLabel: Acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived - the three states of a DoD SAP
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.f makes the nesting operative: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security.' Waived is a strict subset of unacknowledged; there is no such thing as a waived acknowledged SAP.

An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.'

claims.nodeLabel: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 (12 Sep 2024) glossary defines it: 'carve out: A provision approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DCSA of its National Industrial Security Program obligation.'

claims.nodeLabel: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)
claims.text: MAJOR CHANGE, 2024. DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.i.: 'Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) oversight for the administration of the National Industrial Security Program will be phased out in July 2029 in accordance with the carve-out provision.' The 2024 policy therefore schedules a blanket, enterprise-wide withdrawal of DCSA from DoD SAP industrial security by July 2029, rather than a case-by-case carve-out.

claims.nodeLabel: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 requires DoD SAPCO to provide 'DSS confirmation of SAP facilities where the DSS has been carved out of security oversight functions', which means a list of carved-out facilities exists as an agency record.

claims.nodeLabel: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 6 lists 'Proposals to relieve DSS of NISP security oversight responsibilities (carve-out) when required' among the actions that must be coordinated through the DoD SAPCO to the Deputy Secretary of Defense for decision.

claims.nodeLabel: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)
claims.text: A programmed phase-out of DCSA oversight across the DoD SAP enterprise by July 2029 converts the carve-out from an exception requiring SecDef/DepSecDef signature into the default state. If accurate, after that date no independent DoD agency holds a routine inspection right at SAP contractor facilities, and the record of which facilities host which programs stops accumulating in DCSA's system. Reasoning stated from 1.2.i.

claims.nodeLabel: Cover mechanisms - HVSACO, nicknames, unacknowledged locations
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 para 5.d: 'All DoD SAPs must be assigned an unclassified nickname generated in accordance with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Manual 3150.29D ... Unclassified nicknames will be used in the annual SAP report to Congress.'

claims.nodeLabel: DCSA as DoD Cognizant Security Office under the NISP
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.i: 'Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) oversight for the administration of the National Industrial Security Program will be phased out in July 2029 in accordance with the carve-out provision.'

claims.nodeLabel: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 2 para 2.k: DoD SAPCO 'Establishes policies and applicable procedures to satisfy reporting requirements for DSS carve-outs, CFIUS, and treaty matters. Provides DSS confirmation of SAP facilities where the DSS has been carved out of security oversight functions.'

claims.nodeLabel: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
claims.text: DoD SAPCO is simultaneously the office that (a) writes the criteria for reviewing waived programs, (b) confirms which contractor facilities are carved out of DCSA oversight, (c) is the single point of congressional liaison, and (d) must approve any contractor's provision of SAP material to a member of Congress. Those four functions in one office, reporting to the official who signs the waivers, is the structural definition of a closed loop. Reasoning: enumeration of the four responsibilities from DoDI 5205.11 and DoDD 5205.07.

Para 7.2.b.: 'Members of Congress assigned to the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to all DoD SAPs within the respective committee's SAP oversight jurisdiction, except for waived programs.'

claims.text: Para 4.1.a.(2): 'Within 45 calendar days of creation of the SAP project, the CA will submit' the required documentation — establishing an internal 45-day paper deadline for new SAP projects, distinct from the statutory 30-day congressional pre-initiation notice under 10 U.S.C. 119(f).

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)
claims.text: BUDGET PAPER TRAIL. Para 7.2.h. (congressional budget justification materials): waived program justification material goes only to committee staff directors, not to the committees as bodies.

claims.text: Para 5.1.e.(1): 'The use of a polygraph examination as a mandatory access determination requirement must be approved by the Secretary of Defense.' Mandatory-polygraph SAP access is a Secretary-level decision, which makes the presence of a polygraph requirement a marker of a program that reached the top of the department.

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)

A cleared DoD employee cannot lawfully brief even an accessed member of Congress without first routing notice through the SAP's own control office.

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)
claims.text: WHAT MAKES A PROGRAM WAIVED, in DoD's own words. Para 1.2.f.: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security.' The waiver therefore attaches only to programs that are ALREADY unacknowledged; waived is a subset of unacknowledged, not a parallel category.

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)
claims.text: TIER ARCHITECTURE. DoDI 5205.11 establishes a tiered SAP structure: umbrellas at tier 1, compartments at tier 2, sub-compartments at tier 3 and below; only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense may alter tier 1 structures. It distinguishes 'structural SAP: A SAP that provides organization to the architecture and does not protect discrete CPI' from 'content SAP: A SAP that protects discrete CPI.'

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)
claims.text: Para 7.2.f. verbatim: 'The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs.' Non-committee members and staff may be granted access only to NON-waived SAPs, and only 'by the Director, DoD SAPCO following consultation with the respective chamber' (7.2.d.). Senate and House leadership may each nominate one professional staff member for access to all DoD SAPs (7.2.e.).

Congress's own audit arm cannot reach a DoD SAP without the audited department's SAPCO first clearing it with four members.

claims.nodeLabel: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)
claims.text: The structural/content distinction is load-bearing for any search of SAP nomenclature: a structural SAP is a container with a codeword and no content of its own, so a program name appearing in budget or security documentation may correspond to no discrete body of protected information at all. Conversely, discrete CPI can be moved between compartments under an unchanged tier-1 umbrella name without any tier-1 action reaching the Secretary. Reasoning stated from the 1.2 tier description.

claims.text: THE STATUTORY GROUP AND THE DEPARTMENT'S GROUP ARE NOT THE SAME, AND THE DEPARTMENT'S IS WIDER. The statute, 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2), names only 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve seats across six committee entities, and no staff. DoD Instruction 5205.11, paragraph 7.2.a.(3), states verbatim: 'Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' The Department therefore adds two staff categories the statute does not name, and extends the group to the two intelligence committees, which Section 119(g) does not include. Whether that is a lawful gloss or an administrative expansion is a live question the board can put on the record.

Doc. 105-2, 1997, Chapter II, as mirrored by the Federation of American Scientists - https://sgp.fas.org/library/moynihan/chap2.html
claims.text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. None of the four is a public document class. There is no statutory requirement anywhere in Section 119 to report the NUMBER of waivers exercised, the fact that any waiver was exercised, or an aggregate count, to anyone outside those twelve seats. The absence of a public instance is therefore fully explained by the design of the mechanism and is NOT evidence of concealment beyond what the statute itself authorises.

claims.text: THE STRONGEST SINGLE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT THE POPULATION IS NON-EMPTY IS A RECURRING REVIEW REQUIREMENT. DoDI 5205.11 requires that in its annual review the Special Access Program Oversight Committee - chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense - shall assess, among four listed items, '(d) All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' A standing annual agenda item to decide whether waived programs should REMAIN waived is only drafted if waived programs exist. This is a 2024 document, so the finding is current, not historical.

claims.text: The Department's own definition, from the DoDI 5205.11 glossary, verbatim: 'waived SAP - A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' And, adjacent to it: 'unacknowledged SAP - A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A waived SAP is therefore a proper subset of the unacknowledged SAPs, distinguished precisely by the exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver.

The DoD will submit to the congressional defense and intelligence committees such additional materials as are requested by the committees and are within the jurisdiction of each committee. Justification materials for waived programs will be presented only to the committee staff directors.' This is the best available primary evidence that DoD continued to route waived-programme justification material to the defense committees after the 31 December 2021 termination of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) - but note that it routes that material to staff directors rather than through the 119(e)(2) chair-and-ranking channel, and it rests on committee request rather than on a standing statutory reporting duty.

Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' This is materially wider than 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) on two axes: it admits committee staff directors and a security manager, and it extends to the intelligence committees, which have no entitlement under section 119.
